questions.question: A polystyrene bead moves upwards through oil at constant velocity. Complete the free-body force diagram showing all forces on the bead.
questions.answer: Add weight (downwards) and viscous drag (downwards); the upthrust already drawn acts upwards and equals weight + drag
steps: The bead rises at constant velocity, so the resultant force on it is zero.
Weight W acts vertically downwards from the centre of the bead.
Viscous drag acts downwards as well, because it opposes the upward motion.
Upthrust = weight + drag, so the upward arrow must be as long as the two downward arrows added together.

questions.question: A polystyrene bead of diameter 4.00 x 10^-3 m is in oil of density 930 kg m^-3. Show that the upthrust on the bead is about 3.1 x 10^-4 N.
questions.answer: Upthrust = 3.1 x 10^-4 N
steps: Radius r = 2.00 x 10^-3 m.
Upthrust = weight of displaced oil = rho V g = 930 x 3.35 x 10^-8 x 9.81 = 3.06 x 10^-4 N, about 3.1 x 10^-4 N.

questions.question: Stokes' law is only valid if the bead moves sufficiently slowly through the oil. State the reason for this condition.
questions.answer: At higher speeds the flow becomes turbulent, and the drag is no longer given by Stokes' law
steps: Stokes' law assumes laminar (smooth, layered) flow of the fluid around the sphere.
At higher speeds the flow becomes turbulent, with eddies.
In turbulent flow the drag is not proportional to speed, so Stokes' law does not apply.

questions.question: For Stokes' law to be valid the speed of the bead must be less than v_R, given by a formula. The oil viscosity is 4.90 x 10^-2 Pa s and the bead weight is 1.05 x 10^-5 N. Deduce whether Stokes' law can be applied.
questions.answer: Stokes' law cannot be applied: the bead's speed (about 0.16 m s^-1) is greater than v_R = 0.13 m s^-1
steps: From the paper, v_R = 10 x viscosity / (density of oil x diameter) = 10 x 4.90 x 10^-2 / (930 x 4.00 x 10^-3) = 0.13 m s^-1.
At constant velocity upthrust = weight + drag, so drag D = 3.06 x 10^-4 - 1.05 x 10^-5 = 2.96 x 10^-4 N (upthrust from part (b)).
Stokes' law: D = 6 pi eta r v, so v = D / (6 pi eta r) = 2.96 x 10^-4 / (6 pi x 4.90 x 10^-2 x 2.00 x 10^-3) = 0.16 m s^-1.
The bead speed 0.16 m s^-1 is greater than v_R = 0.13 m s^-1, so the flow is not laminar.
Therefore Stokes' law cannot be applied to this bead.

questions.question: A small spherical air bubble moves upwards in water. State the condition needed for Stokes' law to apply to the bubble.
questions.answer: The flow of water around the bubble must be laminar
steps: Stokes' law applies only when the flow around the sphere is laminar.
This requires the bubble to move slowly enough that the flow does not become turbulent.

questions.question: A bubble of volume 5.3 x 10^-11 m^3 moves upwards at constant velocity in water of density 998 kg m^-3. Show that the upthrust on the bubble is about 5 x 10^-7 N.
questions.answer: Upthrust = 5.2 x 10^-7 N, about 5 x 10^-7 N
steps: Upthrust = rho V g = 998 x 5.3 x 10^-11 x 9.81.
= 5.19 x 10^-7 N, which is about 5 x 10^-7 N.

questions.question: The bubble rises at constant velocity 0.035 m s^-1 in water of viscosity 9.5 x 10^-4 Pa s. Ignore the bubble's weight. Deduce whether Stokes' law applies.
questions.answer: Stokes' law does not apply: the Stokes drag would be about 1.5 x 10^-7 N, not the 5.2 x 10^-7 N needed (and Re is about 17)
steps: At constant velocity the drag balances the upthrust (weight ignored): D = 5.19 x 10^-7 N.
Stokes drag = 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 9.5 x 10^-4 x 2.33 x 10^-4 x 0.035 = 1.46 x 10^-7 N.
The actual drag (5.2 x 10^-7 N) is about 3.6 times the Stokes prediction, so Stokes' law does not fit.
Reynolds number Re = rho v d / eta = 998 x 0.035 x 4.66 x 10^-4 / (9.5 x 10^-4) = 17, far above the laminar range.
So the flow is not laminar and Stokes' law does not apply to the bubble.

questions.question: A 35 kg object falls at terminal velocity in seawater of density 1.03 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Its volume is 1.60 x 10^-2 m^3. Show that the drag at terminal velocity is about 200 N.
questions.answer: Drag = 1.8 x 10^2 N, which is about 200 N to 1 s.f.
steps: Weight W = m g = 35 x 9.81 = 343.4 N.
At terminal velocity the resultant force is zero, so drag D = W - U = 343.4 - 161.7 = 181.7 N.
181.7 N is about 200 N to 1 s.f., as required.

questions.question: The drag on the object obeys D = k v^2 with k = 2.2 N s^2 m^-2. Determine the terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Terminal velocity = 9.1 m s^-1
steps: At terminal velocity the drag equals the net downward force found in part (i): D = 181.7 N.
k v^2 = D, so v = sqrt(D / k) = sqrt(181.7 / 2.2) = sqrt(82.6).

questions.question: Give two reasons why Stokes' law could not be used to calculate the terminal velocity of the object in part (a)(i).
questions.answer: The speed is too high for laminar flow, and the object is large (not a small sphere)
steps: The speed of about 9 m s^-1 is too high: the flow around the object would be turbulent, not laminar.
The object is large (35 kg) rather than a small sphere, so Stokes' law for small spheres does not apply.

questions.question: A lift bag with an object is released and accelerates upwards until it reaches a maximum velocity. Explain why it reaches a maximum velocity.
questions.answer: Drag increases with speed until it balances the net upward force, so the resultant force becomes zero
steps: The net upward force (upthrust minus weight) is roughly constant at first.
As the bag speeds up, the drag force increases, opposing the motion.
The resultant force = net upward force minus drag decreases as speed rises.
When drag equals the net upward force, the resultant force is zero, so acceleration stops and the maximum (terminal) velocity is reached.

questions.question: Stokes' law can be used to determine the frictional force on an object moving through a fluid. To which would it best apply? A: large sphere, fast, B: large sphere, slow, C: small sphere, fast, D: small sphere, slow.
questions.answer: D: a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid
steps: Stokes' law applies to small spheres moving slowly, giving laminar flow.
A large sphere (A, B) or a fast sphere (C) breaks the conditions.
Option D meets both conditions.

questions.question: A ball bearing falls at terminal velocity through a liquid. As the temperature of the liquid increases, the terminal velocity increases. Which row of the table is correct?
questions.answer: B: viscous drag constant, viscosity of the liquid decreases
steps: At terminal velocity the resultant force is zero, so drag = weight - upthrust.
Weight and upthrust do not change when the liquid warms (density taken as constant), so the drag stays constant.
Drag = 6 pi eta r v: the same drag at a greater speed v means a smaller viscosity eta, so viscosity decreases as temperature rises.
Rows C and D (drag decreases) and row A (viscosity increases) are all wrong, so B is correct.

questions.question: A water droplet moves downwards through oil with laminar flow around it. State what is meant by laminar flow.
questions.answer: Fluid flows smoothly in layers (streamlines), with no turbulence or eddies
steps: In laminar flow each layer of fluid slides smoothly past its neighbours.
Streamlines are smooth and do not cross, with no eddies or turbulence.

questions.question: State the condition necessary for the speed of the droplet to be constant.
questions.answer: The resultant force on the droplet must be zero (forces balanced)
steps: Constant speed means zero acceleration.
By Newton's first law the resultant force must then be zero, so weight = upthrust + drag.

questions.question: A spherical water droplet has volume 3.35 x 10^-8 m^3 and water density 1.00 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Calculate its weight.
questions.answer: Weight of droplet = 3.3 x 10^-4 N

questions.question: The droplet is completely submerged in oil of density 0.94 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Show that the upthrust is about 3 x 10^-4 N.
questions.answer: Upthrust = 3.1 x 10^-4 N, about 3 x 10^-4 N
steps: Upthrust = weight of displaced oil = rho_oil V g.

questions.question: Calculate the terminal velocity of the water droplet in oil of viscosity 0.11 Pa s, given the droplet volume, weights and upthrust from parts (i) and (ii).
questions.answer: Terminal velocity = 4.8 x 10^-3 m s^-1
steps: At terminal velocity drag = weight - upthrust = 3.29 x 10^-4 - 3.09 x 10^-4 = 1.97 x 10^-5 N.
Stokes' law: D = 6 pi eta r v, so v = D / (6 pi eta r).

questions.question: Which change would decrease the time taken for sand to settle in sea water? A: smaller sand particles, B: lower temperature, C: smaller terminal velocity, D: lower viscosity of the sea water.
questions.answer: D: lower viscosity of the sea water
steps: Shorter settling time needs a larger terminal velocity.
Terminal velocity v is proportional to 1/eta (Stokes' law), so lower viscosity gives a larger terminal velocity.
A smaller particle (A) or a lower temperature (B, which raises viscosity) reduces speed, and C lowers the speed directly.
So D is correct.

questions.question: State one other condition that must be met for Stokes' law to apply to a moving object.
questions.answer: The flow of fluid around the object must be laminar
steps: Stokes' law applies only when the fluid flow around the sphere is laminar.
This means the sphere must move slowly enough that turbulence does not form.

questions.topic: Stokes Law Check For Falling Sphere
questions.question: A steel ball bearing of diameter 6.0 x 10^-3 m and mass 9.1 x 10^-4 kg falls through water at a constant 0.50 m s^-1. The upthrust is 1.1 x 10^-3 N and water viscosity is 8.9 x 10^-4 Pa s. Assess whether Stokes' law can be applied.
questions.answer: Stokes' law cannot be applied: the measured drag is 7.8 x 10^-3 N but Stokes' law gives about 2.5 x 10^-5 N
steps: At constant velocity drag D = W - U = 8.93 x 10^-3 - 1.1 x 10^-3 = 7.83 x 10^-3 N.
Stokes drag with r = 3.0 x 10^-3 m: 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 8.9 x 10^-4 x 3.0 x 10^-3 x 0.50 = 2.5 x 10^-5 N.
The measured drag is about 300 times the Stokes prediction, so Stokes' law does not describe the drag.
The speed is also high, so the flow would be turbulent; Stokes' law therefore does not apply.

questions.question: Which best describes the situations in which Stokes' law applies? A: all spherical objects at low speeds, B: all spherical objects in low viscosity fluid, C: small spherical objects at low speeds, D: small spherical objects in low viscosity fluid.
questions.answer: C: small spherical objects moving at low speeds
steps: Stokes' law needs a sphere that is small and moves slowly, so the flow is laminar.
Option A omits small; B and D refer to viscosity, which is not a condition.
Option C gives both key conditions.

questions.question: A small sphere moves horizontally through a viscous liquid. State the conditions that must apply for Stokes' law to be valid.
questions.answer: The sphere is small and spherical, and the flow of the liquid is laminar (low speed)
steps: The object must be a small sphere, so that its drag depends on its radius only.
The flow around it must be laminar, which requires low speed.
A uniform viscous fluid with no wall or boundary effects is also assumed.

questions.question: A constant horizontal force of 2.3 x 10^-5 N acts on a sphere of diameter 4.5 x 10^-3 m moving through liquid of viscosity 7.1 x 10^-2 Pa s at 5.2 x 10^-3 m s^-1. Calculate the resultant horizontal force on the sphere.
questions.answer: Resultant horizontal force = 7.3 x 10^-6 N
steps: Radius r = 2.25 x 10^-3 m.
Viscous drag (opposing the motion) = 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 7.1 x 10^-2 x 2.25 x 10^-3 x 5.2 x 10^-3 = 1.57 x 10^-5 N.
Resultant = applied force - drag = 2.3 x 10^-5 - 1.57 x 10^-5 = 7.3 x 10^-6 N in the direction of motion.

questions.question: Calculate the maximum speed of the sphere in the horizontal direction, given the same force, diameter and viscosity.
questions.answer: Maximum horizontal speed = 7.6 x 10^-3 m s^-1
steps: Maximum speed occurs when drag equals the constant applied force, so the resultant is zero.
6 pi eta r v_max = 2.3 x 10^-5 N, so v_max = F / (6 pi eta r).

questions.question: A larger diameter sphere in the same liquid is acted on by the same constant force, and the liquid is at a lower temperature. Explain the effect of these changes on the maximum speed.
questions.answer: Both changes reduce the maximum speed: a larger sphere has more drag, and a lower temperature increases viscosity
steps: Maximum speed v = F / (6 pi eta r), so it depends on radius r and viscosity eta.
A larger diameter means a larger radius, so the drag for a given speed increases and v falls.
A lower temperature increases the viscosity of the liquid, which increases the drag.
Both changes increase the drag, so the maximum speed decreases.

questions.question: A falling sphere viscometer measures the terminal velocity of a sphere in a liquid. State why the temperature of the liquid should not increase during the measurement.
questions.answer: The viscosity of the liquid falls as it warms, so the viscosity would change during the measurement
steps: Viscosity depends strongly on temperature, and it decreases as the liquid warms.
If the temperature rises during the measurement, the viscosity changes and the terminal velocity is no longer constant.
So the calculated viscosity would not be reliable.

questions.question: An aluminium sphere of density 2.70 x 10^3 kg m^-3 and diameter 7.00 x 10^-3 m falls through glycerol. Show that its weight is about 4.8 x 10^-3 N.
steps: Radius r = 3.50 x 10^-3 m, so volume V = (4/3) pi r^3 = 1.80 x 10^-7 m^3.

questions.question: The terminal velocity of the aluminium sphere in glycerol was 4.05 x 10^-2 m s^-1. Deduce whether Stokes' law applied, given glycerol density 1.26 x 10^3 kg m^-3 and viscosity 9.50 x 10^-1 Pa s.
questions.answer: Yes, Stokes' law applied: the measured drag (2.54 x 10^-3 N) matches the Stokes prediction (2.54 x 10^-3 N)
steps: Upthrust = rho_glycerol V g = 1.26 x 10^3 x 1.80 x 10^-7 x 9.81 = 2.22 x 10^-3 N.
Drag at terminal velocity = W - U = 4.76 x 10^-3 - 2.22 x 10^-3 = 2.54 x 10^-3 N.
Stokes drag = 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 0.950 x 3.50 x 10^-3 x 4.05 x 10^-2 = 2.54 x 10^-3 N.
The two values agree, and Re = rho v d / eta is about 0.4 (laminar), so Stokes' law applied.

questions.question: State one condition that must be met for Stokes' law to apply.
questions.answer: The flow of the liquid around the sphere must be laminar
steps: Stokes' law requires laminar flow around the sphere.
Other valid answers: the sphere is small and spherical, or it moves at low speed.

questions.question: A scientist uses the viscometer to measure blood, with viscosity 3 x 10^-3 to 4 x 10^-3 Pa s. Explain why a much smaller diameter sphere than the glycerol sphere should be used. Do not include calculations.
questions.answer: Blood is far less viscous than glycerol, so a large sphere would fall too fast for Stokes' law and the timing; a smaller sphere keeps the speed low
steps: Blood has a viscosity about 300 times lower than glycerol (0.95 Pa s).
For the same sphere, terminal velocity would be about 300 times larger, so the sphere would move too fast.
At high speed the flow becomes turbulent, so Stokes' law would not apply.
A too-fast sphere also reaches terminal velocity quickly and falls the measured distance in too short a time to time accurately.
Terminal velocity is proportional to radius squared, so a smaller diameter lowers the speed to a laminar, measurable range.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the terminal velocity of a falling raindrop, including a free-body force diagram at terminal velocity (upthrust negligible).
questions.answer: Terminal velocity is the constant maximum speed reached when air resistance equals the weight, so the resultant force is zero
steps: A raindrop accelerates at first because its weight is larger than the air resistance.
As speed increases, air resistance increases until it equals the weight.
Free-body diagram: weight acting down and air resistance acting up, of equal size.
With zero resultant force the drop moves at a constant (terminal) velocity.

questions.question: Using the air resistance expression for a raindrop of radius 2.0 x 10^-3 m (with density of air 1.2 kg m^-3 and rainwater density 1.0 x 10^3 kg m^-3), calculate the terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Terminal velocity = 7.0 m s^-1
steps: The air resistance is given on the paper as F = 0.45 rho A v^2, with rho the density of air and A the cross-sectional area.
At terminal velocity F = weight = (4/3) pi r^3 rho_water g = (4/3) pi (2.0 x 10^-3)^3 x 1.0 x 10^3 x 9.81 = 3.29 x 10^-4 N.

questions.question: A water drop slides off a leaf. Add to the diagram the positions of the drop at regular intervals of time, given the first two positions.
questions.answer: Further positions go down and to the right along a smooth curve, with the gap between successive positions getting larger each time
steps: The drop is accelerating downwards (free fall, little air resistance), so in equal time intervals it travels further each time.
Each new gap between positions is bigger than the one before it, so the dots spread out.
The sideways speed from leaving the leaf stays roughly constant, so the horizontal spacing stays equal while the vertical spacing grows, giving a curved (parabolic) path.
Mark at least two more positions along this curve, continuing from the two given.

questions.topic: Height Of Leaf From Drop Spacing
questions.question: Water falls from a leaf at five drops per second. As each drop reaches the ground there are four drops above it in the air, and the highest drop has just left the leaf. Calculate the height of the leaf.
questions.answer: Height of leaf = 3.1 m
steps: Drops are released every 1/5 = 0.20 s.
The highest drop has just left the leaf (age 0), and the four drops above the ground drop are at ages 0, 0.20, 0.40 and 0.60 s.
So the ground drop has been falling for 0.80 s.

questions.topic: Conditions For Stokes Law In Investigation
questions.question: A student investigates small ball-bearings falling through a liquid to find its viscosity. State the conditions needed for Stokes' law to apply.
questions.answer: The ball-bearing is small and spherical, and the flow of liquid around it is laminar (low speed)
steps: The ball-bearing must be a small sphere.
The flow of liquid around it must be laminar, which needs low speed.
The liquid should be uniform, with no wall effects, for the standard result to hold.

questions.topic: Free Body Diagram At Terminal Velocity
questions.question: Complete the free-body force diagram for a ball-bearing falling at terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Weight acts down; upthrust and viscous drag both act up, with weight = upthrust + drag
steps: Weight acts vertically downwards from the centre of the ball.
Upthrust acts vertically upwards from the displaced liquid.
Viscous drag acts upwards, opposing the downward motion.
At terminal velocity the upward forces balance the weight: weight = upthrust + drag.

questions.question: A ball-bearing of radius 2.30 mm and weight 4.00 x 10^-3 N falls at terminal velocity 0.0824 m s^-1 in a liquid. The liquid density is 1.26 x 10^3 kg m^-3 and glycerol's viscosity at room temperature is 0.934 Pa s. Deduce whether the liquid is glycerol.
questions.answer: Yes, the liquid is consistent with glycerol: the Stokes drag (3.34 x 10^-3 N) matches the drag from the forces (3.37 x 10^-3 N) within about 1%
steps: Drag at terminal velocity D = W - U = 4.00 x 10^-3 - 6.30 x 10^-4 = 3.37 x 10^-3 N.
Stokes drag = 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 0.934 x 2.30 x 10^-3 x 0.0824 = 3.34 x 10^-3 N.
The two drags agree to about 1%, and Re = rho v d / eta is about 0.5, so Stokes' law applies.
Therefore the liquid is consistent with glycerol at room temperature.

questions.question: An object is moving through a fluid. Which row of the table states the conditions that must be met for Stokes' law to apply?
questions.answer: C: small, spherical, laminar flow
steps: Stokes' law (drag = 6 pi eta r v) is derived for a small sphere moving through a fluid with laminar flow.
Rows A and B (turbulent flow) are wrong, because turbulent drag is not given by Stokes' law.
Row D allows any shape, but the law only holds for a sphere.
Only row C has small, spherical and laminar, so C is correct.

questions.topic: Conditions For Stokes Law Data Logger
questions.question: State the conditions under which Stokes' law applies to an object moving through a fluid.
questions.answer: The object is a small sphere, the flow is laminar, and the object moves at low speed
steps: The object must be a small sphere so that the drag depends only on its radius.
The flow around the object must be laminar, which needs low speed.
The fluid must be uniform and viscous, with no wall effects.

questions.question: The data-logger graph of a falling ball-bearing is shown. Explain the shape of the graph.
questions.answer: The ball starts from rest (zero gradient), accelerates (gradient increases), then the graph becomes a straight line, showing a constant terminal velocity
steps: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is the velocity. At t = 0 the gradient is zero because the ball is released from rest.
Over the first 0.6 s the graph gets steeper: the ball accelerates because its weight is greater than upthrust + drag, but the drag grows with speed, so the acceleration gets smaller.
After about 0.6 s the graph is a straight line, so the velocity is constant: drag + upthrust = weight, the resultant force is zero, and the ball is at terminal velocity.

questions.question: A ball-bearing of diameter 1.6 mm has a difference of 1.45 x 10^-4 N between its upthrust and weight. Calculate the viscosity of the liquid, assuming Stokes' law applies.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 4.6 x 10^-2 Pa s (about 0.046 Pa s)
steps: Terminal velocity is the gradient of the straight part of the graph, e.g. from t = 0.6 s (11.6 cm) to t = 1.1 s (1.3 cm): v = 10.3 x 10^-2 m / 0.5 s = 0.21 m s^-1.
At terminal velocity the drag equals the difference between weight and upthrust, D = 1.45 x 10^-4 N.
Radius r = 0.80 x 10^-3 m. Stokes' law: D = 6 pi eta r v, so eta = D / (6 pi r v).

questions.topic: Effect Of Temperature On Fall Time
questions.question: The liquid was heated and the ball-bearing took less time to fall a given distance. Explain why, assuming the density of the liquid is constant.
questions.answer: Heating lowers the viscosity, so the drag is smaller and the terminal velocity is larger, giving a shorter fall time
steps: Heating the liquid lowers its viscosity.
Lower viscosity means less viscous drag for a given speed (drag = 6 pi eta r v).
The drag balances the same net weight force at a higher speed, so the terminal velocity is larger.
A larger speed covers the given distance in less time.

questions.question: A spherical mass falls through the sea after becoming detached from a diver. State the conditions for Stokes' law to apply.
questions.answer: The mass is a small sphere, and the flow of water around it is laminar (low speed)
steps: The mass must be a small sphere moving through the fluid.
The flow around it must be laminar, which requires low speed.

questions.topic: Stokes Law Check For Diver Mass
questions.question: At terminal velocity the mass fell 25 m in 0.36 s. There was a 4.6 N difference between weight and upthrust. The sphere's volume is 45 cm^3 and the water viscosity is 1.2 x 10^-3 Pa s. Deduce whether Stokes' law applied.
questions.answer: Stokes' law did not apply: Stokes drag would be about 0.035 N, but the measured drag is 4.6 N
steps: Terminal speed v = 25 / 0.36 = 69 m s^-1.
Measured drag at terminal velocity = 4.6 N (weight minus upthrust).
Stokes drag = 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 1.2 x 10^-3 x 2.21 x 10^-2 x 69 = 0.035 N.
The measured drag is about 130 times the Stokes prediction, and the speed is very high, so the flow is turbulent.
Therefore Stokes' law did not apply.

questions.question: The diver was at the sea surface at 0 s. Explain how the v-t graph shows the diver was back at the surface at 82 s.
questions.answer: The area between the graph and the time axis from 0 to 82 s is zero, so the net displacement is zero
steps: The area under a velocity-time graph gives the displacement.
Areas above the time axis (upward motion) and below it (downward motion) between 0 and 82 s must be equal.
Equal positive and negative areas give zero net displacement, so the diver is back at the surface.

questions.question: Determine the vertical acceleration of the diver at 70 s from the velocity-time graph.
questions.answer: Acceleration = -9 x 10^-3 m s^-2 (about 0.009 m s^-2 downwards, the upward velocity is decreasing)
steps: Acceleration is the gradient of the v-t graph, so draw a tangent to the curve at t = 70 s.
Over the curve near 70 s, v falls from about 0.38 m s^-1 at 67 s to about 0.32 m s^-1 at 74 s.
The negative sign means the acceleration is downwards (opposite to the upward velocity); values from -8 x 10^-3 to -1.0 x 10^-2 m s^-2 are acceptable from a graph reading.

questions.question: For which conditions does Stokes' law apply? A: spherical objects and laminar flow, B: spherical objects and low viscosity, C: cylindrical objects and laminar flow, D: cylindrical objects and low viscosity.
questions.answer: A: spherical objects and laminar flow
steps: Stokes' law applies to spherical objects moving through fluid with laminar flow.
Cylindrical objects (C, D) do not fit the derivation of Stokes' law.
Low viscosity (B, D) is not a condition, so option A is correct.

questions.question: A grain of sand quickly reaches terminal velocity when it falls into water. State why the grain reaches terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Drag increases with speed until it balances the net downward force, so the resultant force becomes zero
steps: At the start the weight is larger than the upthrust plus drag, so the grain accelerates.
As speed increases, the drag increases.
Terminal velocity is reached when drag plus upthrust equals weight, so the resultant force is zero.

questions.topic: Stokes Law Check For Sand Grain
questions.question: A spherical sand grain of weight 4.3 x 10^-5 N displaces water with weight 1.5 x 10^-5 N and falls at terminal velocity 0.050 m s^-1. Viscosity of water is 1.2 x 10^-3 Pa s and grain diameter 1.5 x 10^-3 m. Deduce whether Stokes' law applies.
questions.answer: Stokes' law does not apply: the measured drag is 2.8 x 10^-5 N, but Stokes' law gives about 8.5 x 10^-7 N
steps: Drag at terminal velocity D = weight - upthrust = 4.3 x 10^-5 - 1.5 x 10^-5 = 2.8 x 10^-5 N.
Radius r = 7.5 x 10^-4 m.
Stokes drag = 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 1.2 x 10^-3 x 7.5 x 10^-4 x 0.050 = 8.5 x 10^-7 N.
The measured drag is about 33 times the Stokes prediction, so Stokes' law does not apply.

questions.question: Explain how the temperature of the water affects the terminal velocity of a grain of sand if Stokes' law does apply.
questions.answer: Higher temperature lowers the viscosity, which reduces drag and increases the terminal velocity (v is proportional to 1/eta)
steps: Stokes' law gives terminal velocity v = (2/9)(rho_s - rho_w) g r^2 / eta.
Raising the temperature lowers the viscosity eta of the water.
Lower viscosity gives a larger terminal velocity, since v is proportional to 1/eta.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by terminal velocity.
questions.answer: The constant maximum velocity reached when the drag and upthrust together balance the weight, so the resultant force is zero
steps: A falling object accelerates until the drag increases enough to balance the other forces.
At that point the resultant force is zero and the object moves at constant speed.
This constant speed is the terminal velocity.

questions.question: A glass sphere of diameter 35 mm travels at terminal velocity through a liquid of density 1.43 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Glass has density 2.52 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Show that the drag force is about 0.2 N.
questions.answer: Drag = 0.24 N, about 0.2 N
steps: At terminal velocity drag D = W - U = 0.555 - 0.315 = 0.24 N, about 0.2 N.

questions.question: The graph of terminal velocity v against d^2 is shown. Deduce from the graph whether the flow of liquid around the spheres was laminar.
questions.answer: Yes: v against d^2 is a straight line through the origin, so v is proportional to d^2 as Stokes' law predicts, which needs laminar flow
steps: Stokes' law gives v = k d^2 only when the flow is laminar.
The graph is a straight line through the origin, and the points lie close to the line, with no curve at larger d.
So v is proportional to d^2, which agrees with the prediction of Stokes' law, so the flow around the spheres was laminar.

questions.question: Using the student's graph of v against d^2, where Stokes' law gives v = k d^2, determine a value for k.
steps: k = v / d^2 is the gradient of the best-fit line through the origin.
Take a large triangle: at d^2 = 10.0 x 10^-4 m^2 the line gives v = 6.0 x 10^-3 m s^-1.
k = 6.0 x 10^-3 / 10.0 x 10^-4 = 6.0 m^-1 s^-1 (the far end of the line, 7.7 x 10^-3 at 12.9 x 10^-4, gives the same value).

questions.question: The constant k is given by a formula involving the viscosity of the liquid. Using density of glass 2.52 x 10^3 kg m^-3 and density of liquid 1.43 x 10^3 kg m^-3, determine a value for the viscosity.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 99 Pa s (about 1.0 x 10^2 Pa s)
steps: The paper gives k = (rho_g - rho_s) g / (18 eta), so eta = (rho_g - rho_s) g / (18 k).

questions.question: Explain why the top rubber band should be placed a short distance below the surface of the oil.
questions.answer: So that the sphere has reached terminal velocity before it passes the top band and the timing starts at constant speed
steps: A sphere released at the surface first accelerates, so its speed is not yet constant.
Placing the top band a short distance below the surface lets the sphere reach terminal velocity first.
The timed section then has a constant speed, which the calculation of viscosity needs.

questions.question: Another student suggests adding a third rubber band halfway between the top and bottom bands. Discuss the benefit of this.
questions.answer: It lets the student check that the speed is constant (terminal) by comparing the two timed sections, and gives a better average
steps: With three bands there are two timed sections of equal length.
If the two times are equal, the sphere is moving at a constant (terminal) speed.
Averaging over two sections also reduces the effect of timing errors.

questions.question: The student used an equation for the viscosity of the oil with symbols defined in the text. Which quantity is represented by the symbol shown in part (i)?
questions.answer: The weight of the sphere
steps: (4/3) pi r^3 is the volume of the sphere.
Multiplying by rho_s gives the mass of the sphere, and multiplying by g gives its weight.

questions.question: Which quantity is represented by the symbol shown in part (ii) of the viscosity equation?
questions.answer: The upthrust on the sphere (the weight of oil it displaces)
steps: (4/3) pi r^3 is the volume of oil displaced by the fully submerged sphere.
Multiplying by rho_o g gives the weight of the displaced oil, which is the upthrust (Archimedes principle).

questions.question: Which quantity is represented by 6 pi eta r v (written as 6rv in the text) in the viscosity equation?
questions.answer: The viscous drag force on the sphere, from Stokes' law
steps: Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a sphere as F = 6 pi eta r v.
Here eta is the viscosity, r the radius and v the terminal velocity.
So the term represents the viscous drag force on the sphere.

questions.question: The accepted viscosity of the oil is 41 mPa s at 24 degrees C, but the student obtained 36 mPa s. Suggest a possible reason for the lower value.
questions.answer: The sphere had not yet reached terminal velocity when it passed the top band, so the measured speed was too high
steps: Viscosity = 2r^2 (rho_s - rho_o) g / (9v), so viscosity is inversely proportional to v.
If the sphere was still accelerating past the top band, the measured speed is too high.
A larger measured speed gives a smaller calculated viscosity, which matches 36 mPa s being lower than 41 mPa s.

questions.question: Describe a method the student could use to determine an accurate value for the terminal velocity of the sphere in the washing up liquid, using a stopwatch and metre rule.
questions.answer: Mark two points well below the surface, time the sphere over a measured distance once it moves at constant speed, and repeat several times
steps: Release the sphere at the top of the cylinder and mark two points on the cylinder well below the surface.
Use a metre rule to measure the distance between the marks exactly.
Start the stopwatch as the sphere passes the upper mark and stop it at the lower mark.
Repeat several times and average the times to reduce random error.
Terminal velocity = distance / average time, checking the speed is constant between marks.

questions.question: Explain why the use of a larger sphere would increase the percentage uncertainty in the calculated terminal velocity.
questions.answer: A larger sphere falls faster, so it covers the measured distance in a shorter time, and the fixed timing error becomes a larger percentage
steps: Terminal velocity is proportional to radius squared, so a larger sphere has a larger terminal velocity.
It therefore covers the measured distance in a shorter time.
The timing uncertainty (for example reaction time) is roughly fixed in seconds.
A fixed uncertainty in a shorter time is a larger percentage uncertainty in the time and so in the velocity.

questions.question: Complete the free-body force diagram for the sphere travelling at terminal velocity in the washing up liquid.
questions.answer: Weight acts down; upthrust and viscous drag both act up, with weight = upthrust + drag
steps: Weight acts vertically downwards through the centre of the sphere.
Upthrust acts vertically upwards, from the displaced liquid.
Viscous drag acts upwards, opposing the motion.
At terminal velocity the resultant force is zero, so weight = upthrust + drag.

questions.question: The sphere has radius 4.8 x 10^-3 m, weight 3.5 x 10^-2 N, and falls at 0.16 m s^-1 in liquid of density 1.1 x 10^3 kg m^-3. Calculate the viscosity of the washing up liquid.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 2.1 Pa s
steps: Stokes: eta = D / (6 pi r v) = 3.00 x 10^-2 / (6 pi x 4.8 x 10^-3 x 0.16) = 2.07 Pa s, about 2.1 Pa s.

questions.question: A spherical foram of mass 1.15 x 10^-8 kg sinks at terminal velocity in seawater, with upthrust 4.37 x 10^-8 N and laminar flow. Show that the viscous drag is about 7 x 10^-8 N.
questions.answer: Drag = 6.9 x 10^-8 N, about 7 x 10^-8 N
steps: At terminal velocity the resultant force is zero, so drag D = W - U.

questions.question: The foram has diameter 9.2 x 10^-4 m, and seawater has viscosity 1.41 x 10^-3 Pa s. Calculate the terminal velocity of the foram.
questions.answer: Terminal velocity = 5.7 x 10^-3 m s^-1
steps: Radius r = 4.6 x 10^-4 m.
Stokes drag D = 6 pi eta r v, so v = D / (6 pi eta r).

questions.question: As forams sink deeper, the temperature of the water becomes lower. Discuss how the terminal velocities of forams change as they sink deeper.
questions.answer: Lower temperature raises the viscosity of seawater, so the drag increases and the terminal velocity decreases
steps: Viscosity of a liquid increases as its temperature falls.
A higher viscosity increases the viscous drag at a given speed (drag = 6 pi eta r v).
Terminal velocity is reached when drag balances the net weight force, so a larger drag needs a lower speed.
So the terminal velocity of the forams decreases as they sink into colder water.

questions.question: A sphere falls through a viscous liquid. Which row of the table describes the upthrust and viscous drag as the sphere accelerates downwards?
questions.answer: B: upthrust constant, viscous drag increasing
steps: The sphere is fully submerged, so the volume of liquid it displaces does not change and the upthrust (rho V g) stays constant.
Viscous drag = 6 pi eta r v increases as the speed v increases while the sphere accelerates.
Only row B has constant upthrust and increasing drag.

questions.question: A student releases a ball bearing at point V and times its fall to determine its terminal velocity in oil. Which two points (A: V and Y, B: W and Y, C: X and Y, D: W and Z) should be used for the measured distance?
questions.answer: C: X and Y
steps: The ball must be timed only while it is moving at constant (terminal) velocity.
V is above the oil and W is at the surface, where the ball is still accelerating, so a timed section starting there would include the acceleration.
Z is too close to the base of the cylinder, where the ball slows and is hard to time.
X is a little below the surface (ball nearly at terminal velocity) and Y is well above the base, so X to Y is the best measured distance.

questions.question: The graph shows terminal velocity against mass for small spheres of equal diameter falling through a viscous liquid. Which describes the gradient for a liquid of greater viscosity? A: greater gradient, B: smaller gradient, C: variable gradient, D: same gradient.
questions.answer: B: a smaller gradient
steps: For spheres of the same diameter, terminal velocity v = (m g - U) / (6 pi eta r).
The gradient dv/dm = g / (6 pi eta r), which is inversely proportional to viscosity eta.
A greater viscosity therefore gives a smaller gradient.

questions.question: Describe how the student could use her measurements of the ball (mass with a balance, diameter with a digital calliper) and the known density of the liquid to calculate the drag force on the ball at terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Drag = weight - upthrust, with weight from the mass and upthrust from the calliper-measured volume and the liquid density
steps: Measure the mass m of the ball with the balance and calculate its weight W = m g.
Measure the diameter with the calliper, halve it to get the radius r, and find the volume V = (4/3) pi r^3.
Calculate the upthrust U = rho_liquid V g, using the known density of the liquid.
At terminal velocity drag = weight - upthrust, so D = m g - rho_liquid V g.

questions.question: A ball of radius 0.50 x 10^-2 m reaches terminal velocity 5.4 x 10^-4 m s^-1 in a liquid, with drag force 1.1 x 10^-2 N and laminar flow. Calculate the viscosity of the liquid.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 2.2 x 10^2 Pa s (216 Pa s from the given values)
steps: Stokes' law: drag D = 6 pi eta r v, so eta = D / (6 pi r v).

questions.question: A student uses the falling-ball method on vegetable oil. Give one other measurement needed to determine the viscosity of the oil.
questions.answer: The mass of the ball-bearing (to find its weight); the density of the oil is also acceptable
steps: Drag at terminal velocity = weight - upthrust, and then eta = drag / (6 pi r v).
Diameter and the speed (20.0 cm / time) are already measured, so the weight is still needed, found from the mass of the ball-bearing (or its density).
The upthrust also needs the density of the oil, so measuring that is another valid answer.

questions.question: A ball-bearing of diameter 1.24 mm falls 20.0 cm in 1.3 s at terminal velocity. The viscous drag calculated was 5.6 x 10^-5 N. Calculate the viscosity of the oil.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 0.031 Pa s
steps: Radius r = 0.62 mm = 6.2 x 10^-4 m; terminal velocity v = 0.200 / 1.3 = 0.154 m s^-1.

questions.question: The student repeated the experiment with the same oil at a lower temperature. Explain how this affected the time taken for the ball-bearing to fall 20.0 cm.
questions.answer: Lower temperature increases the viscosity, so the drag increases, the terminal velocity falls and the time to fall 20.0 cm increases
steps: Lowering the temperature increases the viscosity of the oil.
A higher viscosity increases the drag on the ball (drag = 6 pi eta r v).
The ball reaches a lower terminal velocity, since the drag balances the same net force at a lower speed.
A lower speed takes longer to cover 20.0 cm, so the time increases.

questions.question: A student releases a metal sphere from rest in oil. Explain why the sphere reaches terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Drag increases with speed until it balances the net downward force, so the resultant force becomes zero
steps: Released from rest, the sphere has no drag, so its weight is larger than upthrust and it accelerates downwards.
As its speed increases, the viscous drag increases.
The net downward force falls as drag rises, so the acceleration decreases.
When drag equals weight minus upthrust the resultant force is zero, and the sphere moves at constant terminal velocity.

questions.question: The sphere falls 0.45 m through oil at terminal velocity in 7.3 s. Radius 0.90 x 10^-3 m, oil viscosity 2.1 x 10^-1 Pa s. Calculate the viscous drag force, assuming Stokes' law applied.
questions.answer: Viscous drag force = 2.2 x 10^-4 N
steps: Terminal velocity v = distance / time = 0.45 / 7.3 = 0.0616 m s^-1.
Stokes drag D = 6 pi eta r v = 6 pi x 2.1 x 10^-1 x 0.90 x 10^-3 x 0.0616.

questions.question: A second sphere with a greater diameter but the same density falls through the same oil at terminal velocity, with Stokes' law applying. Explain how its time to fall 0.45 m compares with the original sphere.
questions.answer: The larger sphere has a higher terminal velocity (v is proportional to r^2), so it takes less time to fall 0.45 m
steps: Terminal velocity v = 2 r^2 (rho_s - rho_o) g / (9 eta) for Stokes' law.
With the same densities and oil, v is proportional to r^2.
A greater diameter gives a larger radius and so a larger terminal velocity.
Time to fall a fixed distance is distance / v, so the second sphere takes less time.
